title: A handful of beans
hook: food shrinks to almost nothing; his spine shows through his belly like a string of beads (MN 36)

segments.voice: Yesterday, holding the breath: the wanderer's head roaring like a blacksmith's bellows. Your line was forcing isn't finding. Where did you stop pushing for a breath? Day forty-five.

There's a statue in the Lahore Museum, in Pakistan, carved nearly two thousand years ago. It shows a man sitting cross-legged in meditation. His face is calm. But his body is barely a body. Every rib stands out. The veins run like cords over his arms. His belly has sunk back almost to his spine. It's called the Fasting Buddha, and people who see it tend to go quiet. It shows the wanderer in the forest near Uruvela, after the breath. Having found that forcing the breath didn't work, he turned to the next great ascetic method. Eat less. Then less. Then almost nothing. Today, a handful of beans.
screen: `A STATUE IN LAHORE.` → `EVERY RIB STANDS OUT.` → `EAT LESS. THEN ALMOST NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Again, the Buddha tells it himself, and he doesn't spare the details. He cut his food down to a single handful a day: a little bean soup, lentils, peas. And his body wasted away. His limbs, he says, became like the knotted joints of vine stems. His backside like a camel's hoof. His ribs stuck out like the rafters of an old, broken shed. The gleam of his eyes sank deep into their sockets, like the gleam of water at the bottom of a deep well. His scalp shriveled like a green gourd left in the sun. When he touched his belly, he could feel his spine. His spine, pressing through, looked like a string of beads. When he tried to rub his limbs, the hair fell out at the roots. People passing by said he was black. Others said he was brown. Nobody could tell anymore. Then he says the line that turns the whole story. By this painful practice, he says, I did not reach anything beyond ordinary human states. No special knowledge. No freedom. Just starvation. Why tell it in such detail? Because in his time, many believed that suffering itself was holy, that the more you denied the body, the closer you came to truth. The Buddha had tried that as far as a human being can, and he reports back honestly: it didn't work. Starving isn't holy. The body isn't the enemy. It's the only place the practice can happen.
screen: `ONE HANDFUL A DAY.` · `A SPINE LIKE A STRING OF BEADS.` · `NOTHING BEYOND THE ORDINARY.` · `THE BODY ISN'T THE ENEMY.` · then, large: `STARVING ISN'T HOLY.`

segments.voice: For this sit, picture your next meal. Or if you have something to eat nearby, take one small bite now and hold it in your mouth. Notice the taste arriving. The texture. The way the body leans toward it, grateful. Chew slowly, much more slowly than usual. Think of the hands that grew it, carried it, cooked it. Swallow, and feel it go down. Your body is being fed. Let that be a kindness, not a guilt. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
A handful of beans. The wanderer's daily food at the height of his fasting, and the proof, in his own words, that starving the body doesn't free the mind.
Your line: starving isn't holy. Today, eat one meal slowly, without a screen, and treat your body as a friend you're feeding. Day forty-five.

howItsDone: Buddhist monks and nuns in many traditions eat moderately, often before noon, as a middle way between indulgence and self-starvation, and the Fasting Buddha image reminds practitioners of the path the Buddha tried and set aside.

fork.setup: you've starved yourself to a handful of beans a day. your spine shows through your belly. has it brought freedom?
options: not yet, so eat even less.
no: nothing beyond ordinary human states.
fork.reveal: he says it plainly: by this painful practice he reached nothing beyond the ordinary. starving isn't holy.

original.note: Pali: the doing of what is hard to do, the name for the Bodhisatta's austerities.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha fasted until he found enlightenment.
what it means: he fasted almost to death, and reported that it didn't work. starving isn't holy.
what a scholar hears: MN 36 gives the similes of emaciation; the Gandhara Fasting Buddha from Sikri (Lahore Museum) depicts it; the commentaries call this period dukkarakārikā, the hard practice.

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the fasting and its similes

notes: MN 36 similes paraphrased (vine joints, camel's hoof, string of beads, rafters, well, gourd, hair falling at the roots, people calling his skin black or brown). Confirm order and wording.
Fasting Buddha from Sikri, Gandhara, Lahore Museum; commonly dated 2nd–3rd century CE ('nearly two thousand years ago'). Confirm.
'Nothing beyond ordinary human states' paraphrases 'no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision'. Confirm.
The practice mentions eating: a Keeper may want a note for listeners with eating disorders or who fast for other reasons.
